independent_mathematics.independent_solution: The electric field supplies carrier energy; carrier interactions transfer it into internal energy. Directed drift is distinct from random thermal motion. Energy can leave for the environment, so generated heat need not equal retained internal-energy increase. Charge is conserved.

option_checks.evidence: Field-driven directed electron motion and interactions with particles supply internal energy; thermal motion can grow during warming. This does not claim that all generated energy must stay in the conductor.

Directed mean drift and random thermal motion are distinct. It also incorrectly places electron drift along the electric field; negatively charged electrons drift oppositely. Either error makes the complete assertion false.
In an energy balance, retained internal-energy increase equals generated thermal energy minus outgoing energy (and any other transfers), so it need not equal the generated amount.
Heating does not require disappearing electrons or consumed charge; the electric field does work on existing carriers. The proposed energy source also omits that work.

independent_mathematics.independent_solution: Q=A=UIt, U=IR and hence Q=(IR)It=I^2Rt. Compare I with R,t fixed, R with I,t fixed, and t with I,R fixed. Fixed U,t instead gives Q=U^2t/R. Only the complete B package satisfies all statements.

option_checks.evidence: (IR)I=I^2R, not IR. For I changing from 1 to 2 at fixed R,t the heat multiplies by 4, not 2. The initial formula and the R/t comparisons are correct, but do not rescue the conjunction.
The starting formula, U=IR substitution, squared current, linear resistance/time factors and all three held-fixed pairs agree.
At fixed U,t, I=U/R makes Q=U^2t/R; doubling R halves Q. The algebra and other comparisons are correct, but the asserted positive resistance proportionality uses the wrong control condition.
Ohm's law is U=IR, not I/R. At fixed I,t the correct heat increases with R rather than decreasing; for I=1 and R=2 the correct U is 2, not 1/2.

independent_mathematics.independent_solution: 30 minutes=1800 seconds. I^2R=5^2*20=500 watts and Q=500*1800=900000 joules.

option_checks.evidence: 5^2*20*30=15000 is the result of treating 30 minutes as 30 seconds; it misses a factor of 60.
5*20*1800=180000 drops one current factor. The actual 5-ampere calculation is five times this value.
5^2*20=500 is power in watts. Labeling it joules and not multiplying by 1800 seconds cannot give the total heat.
25*20*1800=900000 joules, equivalently 900 kilojoules.

independent_mathematics.independent_solution: At the same through-current, local heat rate is I^2R_contact. A stable low contact resistance reduces local heating and an unstable contact can produce intermittent contact. C states the purpose and physical basis.

option_checks.evidence: More contact resistance generates more heat locally at common I; relocating dissipation into the junction cannot prevent that junction from overheating.
The stem fixes the compared current. Importing the fixed-voltage argument that lower R raises I violates that premise; at common I the lower contact R gives lower I^2R.

Improving and stabilizing contact lowers the junction's resistance and its heat rate at common I, and can reduce interruptions caused by looseness. It does not claim zero resistance or authorize repair.
Contact resistance is part of the local I^2R dissipation. Changing or destabilizing it can change heating even if the joint also has a mechanical role.

independent_mathematics.independent_solution: Electrical heat generation can continue while water cooling is removed. A positive imbalance between input power and outgoing heat raises temperature and can cause damage.

option_checks.evidence: Continued electrical input with much weaker heat removal permits internal-energy accumulation and damaging temperature rise; the word 'may' appropriately avoids asserting inevitable failure under every possible condition.
Removing the surrounding water is not cutting electrical supply, and previously dispersed heat does not all return spontaneously to the heater.

Water serves as a heat sink, not an insulator in this fault scenario. Reversing water/air cooling also makes stronger cooling the alleged cause of overheating, inconsistent with net energy accumulation.
The same heating duration need not give the same temperature if heat loss differs. With the same input power, weaker cooling leaves more internal energy in the heater.

independent_mathematics.independent_solution: The same nonzero current flows through all series wires. For equal duration with constant I,R, Q_i=I^2R_i*t. Equal L and S make R_i=rho_i*L/S, so strict actual resistivity order gives strict heat order. The stem deliberately provides no actual resistivity comparison and permits unknown grades and working temperatures, so no universal named-material winner follows. True set B,D.

option_checks.evidence: At common nonzero I and positive t, different rho values imply different R and Q. Equal current removes one factor from the ratio, not the resistance factor.
R=rho*L/S with common positive L,S and Q=I^2Rt with common positive I^2t preserve a strictly greater rho as strictly greatest heat.

The actual material parameters are unspecified. The usual classroom ordering is not a universal theorem over unspecified steel/cupronickel grades and temperatures; the claimed 'certainly' greatest cupronickel heat exceeds what the stated data establish.
A material-name list alone supplies no actual working-temperature resistance order in this explicitly unrestricted comparison; actual resistivities or resistances suffice to identify the maximum.
Series wires have common current, not common individual voltage: U_i=IR_i. At common I,t the least actual resistivity gives least heat, not most.
